claims.text: Adding a small percentage of yttrium to refractory high-entropy alloys improves their high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The untreated initial material is a refractory high-entropy alloy containing no added yttrium.
Yttrium addition causes a protective yttrium oxide layer to form on the alloy surface.
Yttrium reacts with oxygen to form a stable oxide.
The yttrium oxide adheres to the alloy surface.
The adherent yttrium oxide prevents further oxidation of the underlying metal.
After high-temperature exposure in an oxygen-rich atmosphere, the yttrium-containing alloy will have significantly lower oxidation-induced weight gain than the untreated alloy.
The proposed operating conditions are temperatures above 1000°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere.
The untreated-alloy baseline is its oxidation-induced weight gain after 100 hours at 1000°C in oxygen.
The proposed comparison exposes yttrium-containing and untreated samples at 1000°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere for 100 hours.
Equal or greater oxidation-induced weight gain in the yttrium-containing alloy relative to the untreated alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
The hypothesis is restricted to refractory high-entropy alloys and excludes lower-temperature conditions and other alloy types.
The optimal yttrium percentage for maximizing oxygen resistance is unknown.

contradictions.description: The stated working range is above 1000°C, but the baseline and falsification experiment use exactly 1000°C, which lies outside the literal stated range.
The prediction requires a significantly lower weight gain, whereas the falsification rule accepts any lower weight gain without defining statistical or practical significance.
